Chapter 3: The Harm of Coming into Existence
Every life—no matter how lucky—carries its own share of suffering. Some of us face illness, or the pain of losing someone we love. Others struggle with regret, anxiety, or the ache of loneliness. Even the happiest people aren’t immune to pain. It’s not just an unfortunate part of life—it’s how existence works.
Picture a man strolling through a quiet park, thinking back over his years. He recalls moments that make him smile: a child’s laughter, a friend’s encouragement, those feelings of achievement. But woven through those memories are the hard times. The nights spent worrying. The feeling of being lost. The sorrow of saying goodbye to loved ones. Sure, his life’s had plenty of good, but he can’t honestly ignore the suffering he’s felt along the way.
If you ask most people, they’ll say their lives are worth living. We’re naturally drawn to the good stuff, and we find meaning even in struggle. But here’s something to pay attention to: this optimism isn’t always a clear reflection of reality. It’s shaped by the ways our minds help us cope. We’re great at adapting, at finding silver linings, at convincing ourselves things aren’t so bad.
This built-in positivity helps us get by, but it also covers up just how much suffering exists. When we’re thinking about whether to bring someone new into the world, it’s important to look past those comforting illusions.
Giving someone life isn’t just about offering them the chance for happiness. It’s also guaranteeing they’ll face pain. No amount of love from parents, no perfectly safe environment, no lucky circumstances can erase this. Illness, disappointment, loss—even death—are simply part of being alive.
Some folks argue that the happiness in life outweighs the pain, and that’s what makes it all worthwhile. But let’s pause for a second. The real question isn’t whether life can be good—it’s whether it’s right to expose a brand new person to the risk of harm, without them ever having a say. The harm they’ll experience isn’t magically balanced out by the good, simply because they never got to consent to being here in the first place.
Imagine that man again, sitting on a park bench as the sun goes down. He’s grateful for the joy he’s known, but he’s also aware of the cost. He thinks about the people he cares about, and what they’ve been through. He begins to see that bringing someone into existence isn’t just about hope or love—it’s also about risk and harm.
And that changes everything. Procreation isn’t just a private decision. It’s a moral choice, one that comes with real consequences. The harm of coming into existence is real, and it’s something we can’t just look away from.
